name: IPL photofacial

card.summary: Broad-spectrum light flashes used to treat sun spots, redness and broken capillaries; supported for pigment and vascular concerns, less so for wrinkles.
card.aka: Intense pulsed light, photorejuvenation, photofacial, IPL
card.note: Hyperpigmentation and burns are the main reported complications; darker skin tones carry higher risk and manufacturers advise use mainly on light to medium skin.

quick.overview:
An IPL photofacial uses a handheld device that emits short pulses of broad-spectrum light to treat visible skin problems such as sun spots, freckles, redness and small surface blood vessels. Pigment and haemoglobin in the skin absorb the light, heat up and are cleared by the body.

It is a mainstream dermatology and aesthetic treatment rather than a looksmaxxing invention. Reviews describe it as working well for pigmentation and vascular lesions and less well for wrinkles, and home devices are also sold.
quick.mechanism: A flashlamp produces light of roughly 400 to 1200 nm, with filters removing unwanted ultraviolet and long infrared wavelengths. Melanin, haemoglobin and water absorb the energy and convert it to heat, which damages the targeted pigment or vessel while a cooling system protects the skin surface.
quick.risks: Complications reported include hyperpigmentation, temporary redness and microscopic thermal injury; photosensitising medications and existing skin damage are listed as contraindications. A manufacturer cited in one encyclopedia entry recommends use mainly on light to medium skin tones. Regulation varies by country, and a distinction between beauty-grade and medical-grade devices is used in some places.

lead: An IPL photofacial, also called photorejuvenation, is a cosmetic and dermatological treatment that uses intense pulsed light (IPL) to even out skin affected by sun damage, uneven pigmentation, redness and visible small blood vessels. A computer-controlled handheld flashlamp emits brief pulses of non-coherent, broad-spectrum light, roughly 400 to 1200 nm, which targets melanin, haemoglobin and water in the skin. People have it done to look clearer, more even-toned and less flushed, with minimal downtime.[1][3]

Unlike lasers, which emit a single wavelength, IPL devices use interchangeable filters so that one machine can be used for several conditions. The technology was invented by Shimon Eckhouse in 1992, and the US FDA cleared it for vascular lesions in 1995, pigmented lesions in 1996 and hair removal in 1997.[1]

In a study published in Dermatologic Surgery in 2000, 49 people with photodamaged skin received four or more full-face IPL treatments three weeks apart, and more than 90 percent showed visible improvement in wrinkling, texture, irregular pigmentation, pore size and telangiectasias, with minimal downtime and no scarring; 88 percent were satisfied.[3] Reviews of photorejuvenation methods describe IPL as working well for pigmentation and blood-vessel lesions but less well for wrinkles, with limited or anecdotal safety data in places.[2]

angle.text: IPL photofacials are used to fade freckles and sun spots, reduce diffuse redness and broken capillaries, and improve overall tone and texture. A typical course is several sessions a few weeks apart, with little recovery time between them.

infobox: Vascular lesions 1995; pigmented lesions 1996; hair removal 1997[1]
Sun spots, freckles, redness, broken capillaries, rosacea[2]
Four or more sessions three weeks apart[3]

paras: Encyclopedia summaries list photorejuvenation and sun damage (dyspigmentation, sun-related vascular changes, melasma and skin laxity), rosacea and acne-related concerns, telangiectasia and pigmented lesions such as freckles and liver spots.[1][2] IPL is also used for hair removal and for dry eye caused by meibomian gland dysfunction.[1] Wikipedia's page on skin rejuvenation lists dyschromia, rosacea, melasma, acne, photodamage, vascular and pigmented lesions and wrinkles among conditions treated.[2]

A 2004 multi-centre study described IPL as a non-invasive, non-ablative method with minimal adverse events, and IPL is reported to work well for pigmentation and blood-vessel lesions but less well for wrinkles.[2] For hair removal, a 2006 study found no statistically significant difference at six months between IPL, alexandrite and diode lasers, though IPL is generally described as less effective than laser hair removal; typical courses take about 8 to 10 sessions several weeks apart.[1]

A 2000 study in 49 people with photodamaged skin used four or more full-face IPL sessions at three-week intervals and reported visible improvement in wrinkling, coarseness, irregular pigmentation, pore size and telangiectasias in more than 90 percent, with minimal downtime and no scarring.[3] A 2004 multi-centre study of IPL photorejuvenation reported minimal adverse events.[2] A 2006 comparison of IPL with alexandrite and diode lasers for hair reduction found no statistically significant difference at six months.[1]

The most notable complication is hyperpigmentation, and side effects in the 2006 comparison were generally temporary, occurring in 15.3 percent of IPL-treated participants against 28.9 percent for the diode laser.[1] Photosensitising medications and existing skin damage are contraindications, and the treated area should be free of sunburn.[1] Some studies have found that direct heat can damage DNA in treated and nearby cells, causing microscopic thermal injury, and the evidence base includes anecdotal reports.[2] A manufacturer cited by Wikipedia recommends use mainly on light to medium skin tones.[1]

Rules differ by jurisdiction. Some jurisdictions distinguish beauty-grade from medical-grade devices, a distinction Wikipedia notes is sometimes used to avoid regulation. Home IPL devices are sold to consumers.[1]

IPL sits among the light-based skin treatments grouped under hardmaxxing, the more intensive tier of appearance improvement. People pursue it for sun damage, redness and uneven pigmentation, either in a clinic or with consumer home devices.[1]

timeline.event: Shimon Eckhouse invents and patents intense pulsed light.[1]
